title: Sectors and the cycle
desc: Four key sectors and how they tend to fit the economic cycle

cards.title: When times get tough
cards.situation: The economy is slowing and people are cutting back. Which kind of company tends to hold up better?

visual.title: Economic growth · last 6 quarters
visual.label: Economic growth slows from 3.1% to 0.6% over six quarters

options.feedback: Luxury and travel are often the first things people cut when money is tight. A new bag or a holiday can wait.
People keep buying the basics, so staples’ sales usually swing less.
Tech can grow in any economy, but many buyers delay big purchases when money is tight.

cards.work: People still buy toothpaste in a slowdown. A new phone or a holiday can wait.

cards.title: Four sectors to know
cards.text: A **[[sector|sector]]** is a group of companies in the same line of business. Each reacts to the economy in its own way.

items.label: Tech
items.text: Software and chips. Growth-focused, sensitive to rates.

items.label: Energy
items.text: Oil and gas. Moves with energy prices.

items.label: Utilities
items.text: Power and water. Steady, but borrow a lot.

items.label: Consumer staples
items.text: Food and household basics. Bought in any economy.

blocks.tip: A sector fund or [[etf|ETF]] holds many of these companies at once.

cards.title: A simplified cycle
cards.text: Economies grow, slow, shrink and recover. Some sectors have tended to do better in certain phases.

items.title: The economic cycle
items.label: The economic cycle: recovery, expansion, slowdown, recession

cells.text: Banks, tech and shops have often led
Staples and utilities often hold up

rows.note: People cut back, but still buy the basics.

cards.foot: General tendencies, not rules. Every cycle is different.

cards.title: Can you call the cycle?
cards.myth: If I know the phase, I know which sector will win.
cards.reality: Phases are clear only looking back, and every cycle is different. Sectors also move on their own news, like oil prices or rates.
cards.rule: use the cycle to understand moves, not to bet on forecasts.

cards.title: Oil jumps
cards.q: The oil price rises 20% in a month. Which sector feels it most directly?

visual.title: Oil · 1 month
visual.label: Oil rises from $70 to $84 a barrel in a month

options.feedback: Oil and gas companies sell what just got 20% dearer, so their sales move directly with the oil price.
Utilities may pay a little more for fuel, but oil and gas companies’ sales move directly with the oil price.
Staples may face slightly higher transport costs. Oil and gas companies’ sales move directly with the oil price.
Tech may feel slightly higher costs. Oil and gas companies’ sales move directly with the oil price.

cards.work: $70 to $84 a barrel: +20% on every barrel they sell.

cards.title: Rates up, utilities down?
cards.q: Utilities borrow a lot, and many people buy them for steady dividends. When rates rise fast, they often…

options.feedback: Their loans cost more, and bonds now pay more, so their steady dividends look less special.

options.text: Rise: higher rates mean higher dividends
options.feedback: Higher rates don’t raise a utility’s dividend. They raise its borrowing costs and make bonds a rival for income.
Higher rates raise their borrowing costs, and bonds now pay more, so their steady dividends look less special.
Oil matters most to energy companies. Utilities are sensitive to rates because they borrow a lot.

cards.headline: You can see how sectors fit the economy.
lines: A sector is a group of similar companies.
Staples and utilities often hold up in slowdowns.
The cycle shows tendencies, never certainties.
